Which soil is the most sensitive to vibration?
Saturated, loose, uniformly graded fine sand
Steeply graded, fine-grained soils are the most sensitive, especially when saturated. Cohesive and coarse-grained soils are less sensitive.
What happens if the excitation frequency falls within the resonance range of the soil mass beneath the structure?
Resonance: sudden, collapse-like settlement may occur
The soil hardens and settlement stops
Only the superstructure vibrates, not the foundation
The natural frequency must not coincide with the excitation frequency, because that can lead to sudden, collapse-like settlement.
How far do vibrations during construction (piling, sheet piling) typically travel?
At most 20–30 m from the source
These vibrations typically travel at most 20–30 m, but they also affect neighbouring structures – the zone of influence must always be assessed.
What two kinds of damage can vibration cause?
Direct damage to the superstructure, and damage due to compaction of the subsoil
Only a rise in the groundwater level
Vibration can cause damage directly, and damage can also arise from compaction and deformation of the soil beneath the structure.
According to DIN 4150-3, what is the permissible peak particle velocity on the foundation of a residential building for short-term vibration below 10 Hz?
For a residential building 5 mm/s below 10 Hz (20 mm/s for industrial, 3 mm/s for sensitive buildings); at higher frequencies the limit increases.
Why is a high operating frequency (≈ 30–40 Hz) chosen for vibratory driving?
To work well above the natural frequency of the soil–machine system, so that the vibration of the surroundings is smaller
To warm the soil up faster
Because a low frequency does not compact
Above the natural frequency the vibration is not amplified; it is recommended that the operating frequency be at least one and a half times the resonance frequency.
Approximately what is the radius of the settlement crater around a pile driven into loose sand?
Compaction occurs in a zone of radius about 3D, and the surface crater has a radius of roughly 3D + L/2 – this is why it is dangerous if a neighbouring footing is within one pile length.
What is one of the basic rules of machine foundation design?
The operating frequency should differ from the natural frequency of the system by at least 20–30 %
The operating frequency should equal the natural frequency
The machine foundation must be rigidly connected to the floor
The mass of the machine foundation does not matter
Resonance must be avoided; the machine foundation is separated from the floor and the building structure by a movement joint.
